doc.title: Sonny Igoe interviewed by Monk Rowe, Emerson, New Jersey, July 31, 2003

title: Playing and winning the Krupa contest
summary: Igoe jams with Joe Mooney's group and Bobby Domenick, then plays 'China Boy' in the contest and wins.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: about Bobby Domenick. He sat right next to me and said, “listen” [scats] and I was like — I tell you I played with those guys, it was marvelous. And they taught me how to keep time. They really were great with me. They were so tolerant. I say I thought everybody loved me, but I don’t know how I sounded, really. But they were tolerant. They asked me to play all the time. So then we go to this contest. So Gene finally decides, I asked him to sign my snare drum for luck, you know you get it autographed. And I had that head for years, I don’t know what happened to it but I had it for years. Anyway he was so gracious. And I was number three. So they finally decided, “here’s the way we’ll do this. We’ll get a small group from the band, like four or five guys, and play two choruses of the tune with each drummer and the first chorus will be together and then the second chorus will be the drum solo, and then the last eight bars out.” Okay. Well I knew what he was talking about because I’d been playing with these guys.

And they’d say, “Sonny you play the bridge,” or, “you play the last eight.” I knew where it was because I could hear it. So anyway it comes to be my turn, I was number three, he says, “okay now Sonny, what would you like to play?” I was struck dumb. Absolutely dumb. And I said, “gee, I don’t know.” He said, “how about ‘China Boy?’” Well I said fine because I’d been playing “China Boy” for years with his records when he was with Benny Goodman. So I knew the tune backwards and forwards. So he says “you play four bars then they’ll come in.” I said, “okay.” So I [scats] whatever I did, and they came in, and I played through and then I played the solo, and the last eight bars out. I was one of the only ones who knew what to do. The rest of the kids just played solos all the time, they didn’t know how to play in the band.

Keeping time, and I knew when it was time for me to play and when the last eight bars came, they’d go back and they’d all come in again and they all did. And Gene said, “boy they don’t fool around with it up in Ridgewood.” So anyway I figured that by the time they decided who was going to win, they’d forgotten about me, I was number three.

About 40. So anyway Gene brought about six or eight of us up on the stage and I was thrilled to be standing on the bandstand at the Meadowbrook. I had worked there many times after that, but I was like this was big time stuff. So anyway Gene goes down the line, put his hands over this guy and over this guy and over this guy. And I was the last one he came to. And I got the biggest hand. I don’t see how anybody remembered me. And some guys had their own cheering sections there. But still and all, my mother said, “I didn’t think you were going to beat that kid that has all his friends.” And so anyway sure enough, I won the contest and a lot of people heard about it and that sort of thing.
